title: Glera
description: Once called Prosecco itself. The grape behind Italy's famous light, fruity sparkling wine.
L: Glera gives light, delicate wines with pear, green apple, white peach, melon, acacia and wisteria flowers. Acidity is medium to high, body light. Its fresh fruit and floral aromas are best preserved in sparkling wine made by the tank method. It's the main grape of Prosecco.

Until 2009, the grape itself was called Prosecco, after a village near Trieste. When Prosecco became a protected DOC and DOCG in 2009, the grape was renamed Glera, an old local synonym, so that only wines from the defined area could use the name Prosecco. Anyone could plant a grape; no one else can use the place name.
Renamed in 2009 to protect the name
Why was the Prosecco grape renamed Glera in 2009?
To protect Prosecco as a place name
A grape name can be used anywhere; a protected place name can't.

Prosecco is pale lemon, with light, frothy bubbles, aromas of pear, green apple and flowers, and a fresh, light palate. Compared with Champagne, it's fruitier and less bready, with larger, softer bubbles. Most is Extra Dry or Brut.
Yes. It was renamed to protect Prosecco as a geographical name.
Glera gives pear, apple and floral aromas
It's the main grape of Prosecco

Glera grows mainly in the Veneto and Friuli-Venezia Giulia, in north-east Italy. Prosecco DOC covers a large area across nine provinces and must be at least 85% Glera. It's mostly flat land, giving large volumes of fresh, affordable wine. Prosecco Rosé, with Pinot Noir, was allowed from 2020.

Most Prosecco is made by the tank method, also called Martinotti or Charmat: the second fermentation happens in large pressurised tanks, often over a few weeks. This keeps Glera's fresh fruit and floral aromas, without the bready notes of long lees ageing. It's also faster and cheaper than the traditional method.
Match each Prosecco term to its meaning.
Prosecco has its own rules and words.

Prosecco is labelled by sweetness: Brut, up to 12 g/l; Extra Dry, 12 to 17 g/l; Dry, 17 to 32 g/l. Confusingly, Extra Dry is sweeter than Brut. Extra Dry is the traditional style, with a soft touch of sweetness balancing the acidity.
Extra Dry is sweeter than Brut
Which Prosecco is sweeter: Brut or Extra Dry?
Extra Dry has 12 to 17 g/l; Brut up to 12.

Explain why the hills give better wines

Conegliano Valdobbiadene Prosecco Superiore DOCG lies in the steep hills between the towns of Conegliano and Valdobbiadene, north of Venice. The hills, called hogbacks, are so steep that most work is by hand. The area became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2019. Asolo, nearby, is a second DOCG.

Rive are single-village or hamlet crus on the steepest slopes, 43 in total, picked by hand with lower yields. Cartizze, a single hill of about 107 hectares near Valdobbiadene, is the most prized, with some of Italy's most expensive vineyard land. Its wines are traditionally a little sweeter, often labelled Dry.
A prized single hill in Valdobbiadene
Cartizze is Prosecco's top cru, about 107 hectares.

Hillside vineyards drain well, get more sun and cooler nights than the plains, and have lower yields. The wines are more aromatic, more complex and more mineral. Some producers in the hills also make Col Fondo, a traditional style refermented in bottle and left unfiltered, cloudy with lees.
The Conegliano Valdobbiadene hills are a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
Conegliano Valdobbiadene DOCG is Prosecco's hill heartland
Rive and Cartizze are its top crus
Col Fondo is a traditional, bottle-fermented style
Know how long to keep it

Prosecco is Italy's aperitivo wine: with olives, cured ham, fried snacks, cicchetti, Venetian small bites, and light seafood. It's the base of the Spritz, with Aperol or Campari and soda, and the Bellini, with white peach purée, invented at Harry's Bar in Venice. Extra Dry suits slightly spicy Asian food and fruit desserts.

Serve at 6 to 8 degrees. Prosecco is made to drink young, within 12 to 18 months of the vintage, when its fruit is fresh. Unlike Champagne, it doesn't benefit from long ageing. Use a white wine glass to show its aromas, or a tulip glass.
